film.caption: The Last Walk (2:53), November 2026
film.credit: Filmed by Bibiana Juritz and Aram Zadikian, edited by Bibiana Juritz. Sound on; in Italian and English, with English subtitles in the picture
p1: The flag went out for the last time in the Biennale’s final week. On Wednesday 18 November its sections left the pavilion’s water gate by boat, crossed the Bacino di San Marco and were carried by students of the Accademia di Belle Arti into the Academy’s cloister; after an hour there, the boats took them on to Piazza San Marco, where they stood in a line between the columns. On Saturday 21 November, the day before the Biennale closed, the last walk carried them on foot from Tesa 41 to the Piazza and home another way. The Last Walk, filmed by Bibiana Juritz and Aram Zadikian and edited by Bibiana Juritz, is cut from these walks.
p2: A flag is one of the few objects everyone thinks they already understand. People see one and think at once of politics; near the end of the film a young man says so, in Italian: “You see the flag and immediately associate it with politics. In reality the idea is completely different.” A flag is older than any party that tries to claim it. Before it says anything, it is a shared image: a history, a landscape, a way of living, belonging to everyone who has grown up inside it.
fig.piazza: The works carried into Piazza San Marco, 18 November
p3: The units Zadik Zadikian built in Tesa 41 are made to be carried: green, white and red sections that stand on their own feet, each strapped to a frame and lifted onto someone’s back. Set down side by side, they make the tricolore; picked up again, the flag comes apart into people.
q.costerman: “I think Italy is the country most loved abroad. And the only ones who don’t value it are perhaps the Italians themselves.” Leonardo Costerman, 18 November
p4: What the walks met along the way was hesitation. People were moved and curious, and sometimes a little afraid to be seen with the flag. In the film Tony Shafrazi, one of the pavilion’s curators, puts it bluntly: “Italian people are very embarrassed about the flag. Embarrassed: they’re terrified.” His answer is the walks themselves: “Bring the flag to participation. Make it come alive. Not hide it.”
p5: Somewhere along the line, being proud of where you come from turned into something to apologise for. On the walk of 14 November Zadik Zadikian had said it simply: “So far, nobody has come out to honour Italy. We are the first ones.”
fig.selfie: Carriers take a selfie beside a red section, Piazza San Marco, 18 November
p6: The walks were not about borders, and not about being louder than anyone else. This tricolore was made in an Armenian artist’s studio and carried by students of the Venice Academy, through a city where the world’s art gathers every other year. Pride without hostility; belonging without exclusion.
p7: What the walks asked was to carry something heavy together, in public, and to let that weight be seen. On 18 November the works went by boat from the pavilion’s water gate on the Rio delle Galeazze, across the Bacino and up the Giudecca canal to the Zattere, and the students carried them into the cloister, where the hour was for the Academy’s students and staff.

p8: Then the boats took the works across the Bacino to Piazza San Marco. Set down in a line, the flag drew a crowd: people stopped, filmed and asked questions, and for a moment the carriers held each other.
p9: On Saturday 21 November the flag went out one last time, on foot. In the fog the carriers set the sections down in a row before the Basilica, picked them up again and crossed the Piazza in single file, passed the Doge’s Palace and came home along the canal to the Arsenale gate.
fin.home: Home along the canal to the Arsenale gate
q.celant: “All the students are posing at their flag. This is an alive gesture, and I’m grateful to be here for it.” Argento Celant, 21 November
p10: Maybe that is the point. A symbol stays alive only as long as people are willing to carry it, and to keep asking what it means. The walks are over; what they leave is a flag that many hands picked up, carried and set down again.
close: “If I could go back and tell myself one thing, I’d say: throw yourself into things as much as you can. Don’t think; sometimes not thinking is better.” The last words of the film.
